cards.html:
Chapter 7 · Operations: Operate It. A pipeline ends at "deployed". A senior engineer's responsibility ends at "working for users". This chapter covers the part after the green check mark: logs you can query, alarms, service level objectives, ML-specific signals, incidents and postmortems, cost, and what changes when your employer is a regulated German company.

After this level you can:

  • Emit structured logs and turn them into queries, metrics and alarms.
  • Define an SLO, compute an error budget, and use it to make decisions.
  • Monitor a model without labels: proxy signals and a post-deploy distribution check.
  • Run a game day, follow a runbook, and write a blameless postmortem.
  • Estimate cost per prediction, and map your pipeline to GDPR, the EU AI Act and financial-sector rules.

What you build: credit-api with JSON request and prediction logs, model lineage in /health, a distribution check after every deploy, a runbook, a postmortem template, and a game-day story you can tell in an interview.

Every check in Levels 1–4 runs before users see a change. None of them can answer three questions that only production can: Is it up for users right now? Are its decisions still sensible? Did the last change make anything worse? Teams that cannot answer these quickly deploy less often, because each deployment feels risky, which is the vicious circle from Chapter 1. Observability is what makes frequent deployment safe, and DORA's stability measures (change failure rate, recovery time) are measured here, not in CI.

Interview tip

"I don't consider a pipeline finished at 'deployed'. For my credit API, every deploy is followed by a smoke test and a check that the share of rejected applicants is plausible, and I can say from /health exactly which code, model and data are running."

print("prediction done") is useless at 2 a.m. A structured log line is a JSON object with named fields, so tools can filter and aggregate without parsing text. credit-api now writes one line per request and one per prediction (src/credit_api/app.py). Real output:

two log lines (wrapped for print):

{"event": "request", "request_id": "7c1e", "method": "POST",
 "path": "/predict", "status": 200, "latency_ms": 39.7,
 "app_version": "3f2a1c0"}
{"event": "prediction", "risk": "bad", "probability_bad": 0.5893,
 "unknown_categories": ["purpose"], "unknown_count": 1,
 "model_version": "credit-risk/v1"}

Three design choices matter more than the library:

  • A request ID. The middleware takes X-Request-ID from the caller or creates one, returns it in the response, and puts it on every log line. A customer complaint with that ID leads straight to the right lines, across services.
  • Versions on every line. app_version and model_version let you split any metric by deployment: "did errors start with 3f2a1c0?"
  • No personal data. The prediction line contains the decision, not the applicant. Age, amount and employment are personal data under GDPR; logging them needs a purpose, a retention period and access control. Log what you need to operate, nothing more.

ECS sends stdout to CloudWatch Logs. CloudWatch Logs Insights discovers JSON fields automatically, so you can query them directly:

Logs Insights queries:

# p95 latency and request count, per 5 minutes
fields latency_ms
| filter event = "request" and path = "/predict"
| stats pct(latency_ms, 95) as p95, count(*) as n by bin(5m)

# decisions per hour: is the share of 'bad' stable?
filter event = "prediction"
| stats count(*) as n by risk, bin(1h)

# how often do we see categories the model never learned?
filter event = "prediction" and unknown_count > 0
| stats count(*) by bin(1d)

A query answers a question you ask; an alarm asks it for you. A metric filter turns matching log lines into a CloudWatch metric, and an alarm watches the metric:

terminal:

aws logs put-metric-filter --log-group-name <group> \
  --filter-name http-5xx \
  --filter-pattern '{ $.event = "request" && $.status >= 500 }' \
  --metric-transformations \
  metricName=Http5xx,metricNamespace=credit-api,metricValue=1,defaultValue=0
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name credit-api-5xx \
  --namespace credit-api --metric-name Http5xx --statistic Sum \
  --period 300 --evaluation-periods 1 --threshold 5 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions <sns-topic-arn>        # e-mail or chat via SNS

(These commands were checked against the AWS CLI reference but not run for this book; the group name comes from ECS → service → Logs.) Two more alarms complete a minimal setup: p95 latency above your SLO threshold, and no traffic at all when traffic is expected (a broken client looks exactly like a quiet day). Also set a retention period on the log group (aws logs put-retention-policy --retention-in-days 30): cheaper, and GDPR asks you to keep data no longer than needed.

What if… an alarm fires every night and everyone ignores it?

What happens: The p95 alarm fires daily at 02:00 during the batch import; after a week, nobody looks. Then a real incident fires the same alarm.

What you do: An alarm nobody acts on is worse than no alarm: it trains people to ignore alarms. Every alarm needs a runbook entry (what to do) and must be actionable. Fix the cause, change the threshold or window with a written reason, or delete it. Review alarm history monthly.

"The service should be reliable" cannot be measured. A service level indicator (SLI) is a measurement; a service level objective (SLO) is a target for it over a window:

Concept: An SLO for credit-api

SLI: the share of /predict requests that return a non-5xx answer in under 300 ms, measured at the load balancer or from our logs. SLO: 99.5 % over a rolling 28 days. Error budget: the 0.5 % that may fail. At steady traffic that is 0.005 × 28 days × 24 h = 3.36 hours of "bad" per 28 days.

The budget turns arguments into arithmetic. While budget remains, the team ships features at full speed; deployments are allowed to consume some of it. When the budget is spent, an agreed error budget policy applies, for example: only reliability work and fixes are deployed until the window recovers. Product and engineering agree on the policy before it is needed, which removes the "can we ship this Friday?" debate.

Alert on how fast the budget burns, not on single errors. If the service burns budget 14 times faster than sustainable for an hour, a person must look now (page); a slow burn over days becomes a ticket. Pick SLOs from what users need and what you can measure today; 99.5 % for an internal scoring API is a defensible start, "five nines" for a one-person project is not.

Interview tip

"I define the SLO before the dashboards: 99.5 % of predictions under 300 ms over 28 days gives an error budget of about 3.4 hours. Burn-rate alerts page on fast burn; slow burn becomes a ticket. If the budget is gone, we freeze features, not people."

cards.s: Watching the model, not only the service
cards.html:
HTTP metrics stay green while a model makes bad decisions. The hard part for credit models is label delay: whether a loan defaults is known months later. Until then you watch proxies:

SignalCatchesWhere
Share of risk = bad per hourThreshold or model bugs, broken inputs, sudden population changeLogs Insights, alarm
Mean probability_badSlow shifts the share hidesLogs
Share of unknown categoriesUpstream changes (new products, renamed values)Logs, alarm
Input drift (KS, PSI) vs. training dataPopulation change before it hurtsNightly job (Chapter 6)
Real performance (AUC on matured loans)The truth, months lateMonthly job

cards.s: Watching the model, not only the service
cards.sub: The distribution check after every deploy
cards.html:
The cheapest proxy runs inside the pipeline. scripts/distribution_check.py sends 200 reference applicants from the committed data set to the freshly deployed service and checks that the share predicted "bad" lies between the bounds in metrics/thresholds.json (10–50 %; the true rate in the data is 30 %, and the current model predicts 28 % on these applicants):

scripts/distribution_check.py (excerpt):

def bad_share(post: Post, rows: list[dict[str, object]]) -> float:
    risks = [post(row)["risk"] for row in rows]
    return sum(r == "bad" for r in risks) / len(risks)

def check(share: float, lo: float, hi: float) -> list[str]:
    if share < lo:
        return [f"share of 'bad' {share:.2f} below {lo} (approving too many?)"]
    if share > hi:
        return [f"share of 'bad' {share:.2f} above {hi} (rejecting too many?)"]
    return []

cards.s: Watching the model, not only the service
cards.sub: The distribution check after every deploy
cards.html: It runs right after the smoke test in staging and production (_deploy-env.yml, lines 64–67). It is the minimal version of an ML-aware canary: not "does it answer?" but "are its answers plausible?".

cards.s: Game day: the release that passed every check
cards.html:
A game day is a planned exercise in which you break something on purpose to test detection, runbook and people. Run this one; it becomes your answer to "tell me about an incident".

The scenario. A colleague wants fewer false rejections and opens a PR that changes the default DECISION_THRESHOLD in app.py from 0.5 to 0.99. We ran exactly this change locally:

expected output:

$ uv run pytest -q
31 passed in 1.90s
$ uv run python -m credit_api.gate metrics/metrics.json
QUALITY GATE PASSED
$ python3 scripts/smoke_test.py http://localhost:8099 dev
smoke test passed: {'status': 'ok', ...} {'risk': 'good', ...}
$ python3 scripts/distribution_check.py http://localhost:8099 200
predicted 'bad' share on 200 reference applicants: 0.00
DISTRIBUTION CHECK FAILED: share of 'bad' 0.00 below 0.1
  (approving too many?)

cards.s: Game day: the release that passed every check
cards.html:
Every traditional check is green: the tests, the model gate (which evaluates the model, not the serving threshold), the smoke test. The service now approves every applicant. Only the distribution check sees it. With the threshold restored, the same check reports 0.28 and passes.

The exercise in AWS. Merge the change. Watch staging deploy, the distribution check fail, and production never be reached. Then, as if the check had not existed, practise the runbook (docs/runbook.md): freeze deploys, find the bad change from /health and the deploy history, revert it, and time each step. Finally write the postmortem with docs/postmortem-template.md.

What if… the postmortem concludes "the developer should have been more careful"?

cards.s: Game day: the release that passed every check
cards.html:
Then it has failed. People will always make changes like this one; the question is why the system let it through. Here: the threshold is a business decision, but it lived in code without a test or an owner; no check looked at decisions, only at the model. Good action items are prevent (move the threshold into thresholds.json, owned via CODEOWNERS), detect (the distribution check), and mitigate (rollback in two minutes). Blameless does not mean nobody is responsible; it means you fix the system, so the next person cannot make the same mistake.

Interview tip: The incident story, in STAR form

cards.s: Game day: the release that passed every check
cards.html: "Situation: in my credit-risk project I ran a game day: a PR moved the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.99. Task: find out whether my pipeline would catch a release that is technically fine but approves everyone. Action: all 31 tests, the model gate and the smoke test passed, so I added a post-deploy check that sends 200 reference applicants and fails if the rejection share leaves 10–50 %. Result: the bad release stops in staging; I also wrote a runbook and moved the threshold under code ownership. The lesson: test the decisions, not only the model."

A runbook is the page you open when an alarm fires: what the alarm means, the first three commands, how to roll back, who to call. It is written calmly, in advance, by the person who knows the system, for the person who does not. docs/runbook.md is a one-page example; keep it next to the code so it changes with the code.

A postmortem (German teams often say Post-Mortem or Nachbetrachtung) is written after every incident that used error budget or surprised someone. The template in docs/postmortem-template.md has the usual parts: summary, impact, timeline, root cause and contributing factors, what went well, and action items with an owner and a date. Action items without owners are wishes.

Cloud cost is an engineering metric. Three habits are enough at this scale:

  • Tag everything (project=credit-api, env=staging) and activate the tags as cost allocation tags in Billing, so Cost Explorer can split the bill by project and environment.
  • One budget per environment or team, as in Section 5.1, with alerts to the people who can act.
  • Know your unit cost. Our production environment costs roughly 1 USD per day (estimate from Section 5.4: load balancer, one small task, public IPs), about 30 USD per month, almost all of it fixed.

Monthly predictions (assumed)Cost per 1,000 predictions
100,000≈ 0.30 USD
1,000,000≈ 0.03 USD
10,000,000≈ 0.003 USD (more tasks needed; still small)

At low volume, fixed costs dominate, so the lever is fewer always-on resources (shared load balancer, scale to zero for dev, deleting idle staging at night), not faster code. CI costs follow the same logic: free for public repositories; for private ones, the minutes of the slowest jobs times the number of PR pushes. The LLM evaluation from Chapter 6 costs under one cent per full run, so 30 nightly runs stay below 0.30 USD per month; print the estimate in the job summary so a regression in cost is as visible as a regression in quality.

cards.s: Compliance in a regulated German company
cards.html: Banks, insurers and health companies will ask how your pipeline fits their rules. You do not need to be a lawyer; you need to show that your pipeline already produces the evidence those rules ask for. The legal details below are a starting point, not legal advice; dates and articles change, so verify them with your employer's compliance team.

cards.s: Compliance in a regulated German company
cards.html:
RequirementEvidence your pipeline produces
Change management, four-eyes principle (Vier-Augen-Prinzip)Protected main, required reviews, CODEOWNERS, production approvals by a second person, the GitHub deployment history.
Traceability: what ran when?Lineage chain (Chapter 6): commit, data hash, model version, image digest, deployment.
Technical documentationModel card, ADRs, README, all versioned with the code.
Accuracy and robustnessMetric gates, slice gates, behavioural tests, the variance measurement.
Record-keeping / loggingStructured logs with versions and request IDs, with a defined retention period.
Human oversightManual production approval; the runbook; the ability to stop and roll back.

cards.s: Compliance in a regulated German company
cards.html:
The regulations behind the table, briefly:

  • GDPR (DSGVO). No real personal data in test fixtures, golden sets or logs without a legal basis; data minimisation and retention limits. Automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects on people (a loan rejection) are regulated (Art. 22), and high-risk processing needs a data protection impact assessment (Datenschutz-Folgenabschätzung, Art. 35). If an LLM provider processes personal data, where it is processed matters; check your provider's data-residency options.
  • EU AI Act. Credit scoring of natural persons is listed as a high-risk use (Hochrisiko-KI-System). Obligations for high-risk systems include risk management, data governance, technical documentation, automatic logging, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy and robustness. The application dates for high-risk systems have been the subject of political change; verify the current timeline.

cards.s: Compliance in a regulated German company
cards.html:
• DORA, the regulation. In the financial sector, "DORA" usually means the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, which applies since January 2025: ICT risk management, incident classification and reporting, resilience testing, third-party (cloud) risk. Do not confuse it with the DevOps metrics in Chapter 8 in an interview at a bank; mentioning both, correctly, is a strong signal. German supervisory expectations (BaFin) add to this; ask what your employer follows.
  • Works council (Betriebsrat). Systems that can monitor employees' behaviour or performance are subject to co-determination in Germany. A RAG assistant that logs employees' questions (our rag-api) is a typical case: expect the works council to have a say in what is logged and who can read it.

Interview tip

cards.s: Compliance in a regulated German company
cards.html:
"I'd map the pipeline to the controls the auditors already have: PR reviews and production approvals are our four-eyes evidence, the lineage chain answers 'what ran when', and the logs carry versions but no applicant data. For a credit model I'd also ask early whether the AI Act's high-risk obligations and DORA apply."

Exercise: Your first alarm

Deploy credit-api to staging, create the http-5xx metric filter and alarm, and make it fire on purpose (hint: what does /predict return when the model file is missing? Which status code does that produce, and does it count?). Then write the runbook entry for it.

Exercise: Budget arithmetic

cards.s: Compliance in a regulated German company
cards.html:
Your SLO is 99.9 % over 30 days. How many minutes of full outage does the error budget allow? A deployment causes 4 minutes of 50 % errors. How much budget did it consume?

Exercise: Run the game day

Run the threshold game day locally (change the default, start uvicorn, run scripts/distribution_check.py). Then fill in the postmortem template as if it had reached production at 10:47 and been rolled back at 11:20.

Checkpoint: you should now be able to…

cards.s: Compliance in a regulated German company
cards.html:
• emit structured logs with request ID and versions, without personal data, and query them with Logs Insights;
  • turn a log pattern into a metric and an alarm, and keep alarms actionable;
  • define an SLI and SLO, compute the error budget, and explain burn-rate alerting and an error budget policy;
  • monitor a model under label delay with proxy signals and a post-deploy distribution check;
  • run a game day, use a runbook, and write a blameless postmortem;
  • estimate cost per 1,000 predictions, and map the pipeline to GDPR, the EU AI Act, DORA and the works council.
